column2: For Q=100-2P at P=20, Q=60 and absolute point elasticity is 2/3; an arc elasticity between two prices is a different calculation using a specified averaging convention.
column3: At that point, absolute elasticity is 3/2 because quantity divided by price is the elasticity even without applying the demand slope.

column2: For a small price increase on a downward-sloping demand curve, total revenue falls in an elastic region and rises in an inelastic region, with other demand determinants unchanged.
column3: A price increase raises total revenue in the elastic region because the higher price outweighs the larger proportional quantity reduction.

column2: At a differentiable point with absolute elasticity one, MR is zero; the revenue maximum need not be the profit maximum when marginal cost is positive.
column3: Unit elasticity makes profit maximal because zero MR automatically equals any positive marginal cost.

column1: AR and MR under linear demand
column2: With inverse demand P=100-2Q, AR has slope -2 and MR slope -4, meeting the price axis at the same intercept.
column3: The MR curve has the same slope -2 as AR and meets the quantity axis at the same output.

column2: A positive cross-price elasticity suggests substitutes, while negative income elasticity classifies a good as inferior; neither coefficient alone determines its own-price elasticity.
column3: A negative income elasticity establishes that the good has positive cross-price elasticity with every competing product.

column2: A consumer-income change shifts the demand schedule, while a change in the product's own price causes movement along the schedule when other determinants are fixed.
column3: An own-price decrease shifts demand outward even when income, tastes and other prices are held constant.

column2: For an interior differentiable optimum with both goods consumed, MRS equals the price ratio; the tangency condition requires the usual convexity and feasibility conditions.
column3: Tangency is sufficient for a maximum regardless of indifference-curve curvature or whether the point lies within the budget set.

column2: For utility U=X+2Y and prices pX=3, pY=4 with positive income, Y offers higher utility per rupee, so the optimum spends all income on Y in this model.
column3: The optimum necessarily divides expenditure equally because both goods have constant marginal utility.

column2: For U=min(X,2Y), positive prices and income lead to a kink optimum satisfying X=2Y when both are purchased.
column3: That utility requires X=Y at every optimum because complementary goods must be consumed in equal physical units.

column2: For a normal good, the substitution and income effects of its own-price reduction both support a quantity increase under the standard decomposition.
column3: For a normal good, the income effect of a price reduction necessarily offsets the substitution effect by reducing consumption.

column2: A Giffen good is inferior in the standard account and requires an opposing income effect strong enough to dominate the substitution effect; being inferior alone is insufficient.
column3: Every inferior good is Giffen because its negative income elasticity makes its demand slope upward.

column2: When positive marginal product is below average product, average product falls; marginal product reaches average product at an interior maximum of average product under usual smoothness.
column3: Average product rises whenever marginal product is positive, even if marginal product is below average product.

column2: In the standard short-run production account, Stage II begins where average product is maximised and ends where marginal product becomes zero.
column3: Stage II begins where marginal product first reaches its own maximum and ends where average product becomes zero.

column1: Returns to scale versus diminishing returns
column2: Doubling all inputs and more than doubling output indicates increasing returns to scale; diminishing marginal returns concern changing one input while others are fixed.
column3: Diminishing marginal returns rule out increasing returns to scale because the two laws vary the same set of inputs.

column2: For Q=K^0.4 L^0.7, scaling both inputs by t scales output by t^1.1, indicating increasing returns to scale in the specified model.
column3: The model has decreasing returns to scale because each individual exponent is below one.

column2: A change in fixed cost alone changes average total cost and profit but leaves marginal cost unchanged when the variable-cost schedule is unchanged.
column3: A higher fixed cost shifts marginal cost upward by the same amount at every output.

column2: When MC is below AVC, AVC falls; MC equals AVC at its interior minimum under standard differentiability assumptions.
column3: AVC falls only when MC is negative, irrespective of MC's position relative to AVC.

column2: A competitive firm with price below minimum AVC shuts down in the short run under the standard avoidable-variable-cost model, even though fixed cost remains payable.
column3: The firm continues whenever price exceeds average fixed cost because fixed costs are unavoidable.

column2: A competitive firm can minimise short-run loss by operating when price covers AVC but falls below ATC, provided output is chosen on the relevant rising MC segment.
column3: Price below ATC requires shutdown even if the firm covers all variable costs and contributes toward fixed cost.

column2: With free entry, comparable firms and no special rents in the standard model, long-run equilibrium can yield zero economic profit while including normal return in cost.
column3: Zero economic profit means owners earn no normal return and total revenue is necessarily zero.

column2: A monopolist with P=100-Q and constant MC=20 selects Q=40 and P=60 in the unconstrained continuous-output model.
column3: That monopolist selects Q=80 and P=20 because monopoly profit is maximised where demand price equals marginal cost.

column2: With positive MC and an interior monopoly optimum satisfying MR=MC, demand is elastic at that optimum in the standard differentiable model.
column3: A monopolist with positive MC chooses an inelastic point because price can then rise without reducing revenue.

column2: Separate markets, no profitable resale and the usual interior conditions lead to equalised marginal revenues; the less elastic market can bear the higher optimal price for common MC.
column3: The more elastic market necessarily bears the higher optimal price because it contributes a larger quantity.

column2: Under the idealised perfect-information model, first-degree discrimination can capture consumer surplus and expand output to the quantity where willingness to pay equals MC.
column3: First-degree discrimination preserves the same consumer surplus as uniform monopoly pricing because only the payment schedule changes.

column2: Free entry can eliminate economic profit while a firm retains a downward-sloping demand curve and operates with excess capacity in the standard long-run model.
column3: Elimination of economic profit makes each firm's demand horizontal and requires production at minimum ATC.

column2: In the standard kinked-demand account, rivals matching price cuts but not rises makes demand relatively less elastic below the kink than above it.
column3: That rival response makes demand more elastic below the kink because every price cut goes unmatched.

column2: A dominant firm's residual demand depends on market demand less the fringe's supply; using total market demand as its own demand can misstate the leader's optimum.
column3: The leader maximises profit using total market demand without accounting for the fringe because followers cannot supply any output.

column2: Penetration seeks rapid adoption through a relatively low initial price, whereas skimming uses a relatively high initial price to capture willingness to pay before later adjustments.
column3: A high initial price aimed at early high-value buyers is penetration pricing because it recovers development costs quickly.

column2: When service demand peaks against capacity constraints, differentiated prices can reflect time-specific scarcity and capacity costs rather than identical marginal costs at all times.
column3: Peak-load pricing requires the peak price to be lower because the larger peak quantity always lowers capacity cost per additional user.

column2: In a differentiable linear-demand example, sales revenue is maximised at MR=0, whereas profit with positive MC is maximised at a lower output satisfying MR=MC.
column3: With positive MC, maximising sales revenue and maximising profit give the same output because both objectives use total revenue.
